questions.prompt:
Twenty welds were made on plates 2 to 21 mm thick, and a line was fitted to the weld time against the thickness (R² = 0.92). Here are its residuals against the fitted values. Which assumption does the plot call into question?
[[figure: st.m13.foundations.funnel 2]]
options: Linearity: the residuals follow a curve, so the line is the wrong shape
Equal variance: the residuals spread wider as the fitted time grows
Normality: the residuals are too few to come from a normal distribution
None: the residuals sit on both sides of zero, so the model is fine
questions.explanation: The points form a funnel: within about ±2 s of zero at the short welds, and out to about ±6 s at the long ones. The spread of the errors grows with the size of y, so the equal-variance (homoscedasticity) assumption fails. Residuals on both sides of zero are not enough; the spread must be the same along the whole plot. A funnel often means the error is proportional to y; item 13.6 shows how a log of y can even it out.

questions.prompt:
A water heater was run at 14 power settings and a line was fitted to the temperature rise against the power (R² = 0.84, slope p < 0.0001). Here are the residuals against the fitted values. What do they say?
[[figure: st.m13.foundations.curve 2]]
options: The relation bends, so a straight line is the wrong form for these data
The error spread grows along the plot, so the variances are unequal
One observation is an outlier, and without it the line would fit well
The residuals look random, so the line is a valid model for the heater
questions.explanation: The residuals make an arch: negative at both ends (−16.4 °C at the lowest power, −9.7 °C at the highest) and positive in the middle, up to +9.1 °C. That is curvature the line misses: the temperature rise levels off at high power. The linearity assumption fails. The first point's residual is large, but it belongs to the arch, not to a single wild value. A small slope p-value only says that x and y are related; it says nothing about the shape.

questions.prompt:
Sixteen loads were applied to a test beam and a line was fitted to the deflection against the load (R² = 0.97). Here are the residuals against the fitted values. What do they say?
[[figure: st.m13.foundations.random 2]]
options: The residuals curve upward, so a quadratic term is needed
The residuals fan out, so the error grows with the deflection
The residuals form a band with no pattern, so no assumption is in doubt
The residuals are all within ±2 mm, so the model must be perfect
questions.explanation: The residuals scatter between about −1.3 and +1.1 mm with no curve, no funnel and no point far from the rest. That is what a valid straight-line model looks like. It is not 'perfect': the residuals are the scatter the model cannot explain, and σ̂ measures it. A pattern-free plot says the model's form and assumptions are reasonable, nothing more.

questions.prompt: A line fitted to 30 observations has R² = 0.96 and a slope p-value of 0.0001. Which of these can still be true? Choose every one that can.
options: The relation between x and y is curved
The spread of the residuals grows tenfold across the range of x
One observation is steering the slope
The model predicts new observations much worse than it fits these
questions.explanation: All four. R² measures how much of y's variation the line explains, and the p-value whether there is any linear relation; neither checks the form, the equal-variance assumption, the influence of single points, or how the model does on new data. A curved relation often has a high R² (the braking Example had 0.98). That is why validation looks at the residuals and at cross-validation, not only at R².

questions.prompt: Match each assumption with the pattern in the residuals that breaks it.

pairs.right: A U shape or an arch against ŷ
A funnel: the spread changes along ŷ
Long runs of one sign in time order
A Q–Q plot that bends away from its line

questions.explanation: Each assumption has its own picture. Curvature against ŷ means the form is wrong; a changing spread means unequal variances; runs in time order mean the errors are related; a bent normal Q–Q plot (item 13.2) means the errors are not normal.

questions.prompt: A model fits its own 40 observations closely and every residual check is clean. A colleague asks whether it will predict next month's production as well. Which half of validation is her question about, and which tool answers it?
options: Reliability, answered by the residual plot of the fitted model
Reliability, answered by the slope's t-test and its p-value
Generalizability, answered by testing on rows the model did not see
Generalizability, answered by a higher R² on the same 40 rows
questions.explanation: How the model does on new data is generalizability. The residual checks say the model describes its own data soundly (reliability), but a model can fit its own data well and still predict new data poorly. Only rows the model was not fitted to can show that: a hold-out test set or cross-validation (item 13.4). R² on the same rows is the optimistic number.
